 Boon, Greenberg unveil plans for independent forum 
 Cricket Australia has declared it will re-hear testimonies from those involved in the 2018 ball-tampering scandal in what it hopes will be a "circuit-breaker" to the rumbling controversy over events from the South Africa tour.
 David Boon and Todd Greenberg, CA's chair and chief executive respectively, today revealed an "independent forum" would be opened in which players and staff who toured South Africa eight years ago can give their version of events in a "confidential environment". It comes after the CA Board met on Tuesday evening.
 The publication of Usman Khawaja's autobiography, Sabr , has sparked a frenzy of claims and counter-claims relating to the Cape Town incident that saw David Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft all receive heavy penalties.  
 Speaking in Hobart on Thursday, Greenberg insisted CA is not "re-prosecuting" the initial investigation of ball-tampering by Australia in the third Test against the Proteas at Newlands.  
 He said no new sanctions would be handed down; that what is revealed in the forum run by an independent senior lawyer or former judge would be confidential; and that it would be up to the CA Board what is made public at the end of a process expected to take about a month.  
 "We will look to be as transparent as we possibly can, whilst at the same time protecting the confidentiality of the people who come forward," said Greenberg, who conceded "the game is hurting at the moment" in hearing the "conflicting accounts of what transpired in Cape Town in 2018".
 He added: "It is not good for anyone. We need to find a path through and we need to heal."
 While Warner, Smith and Bancroft were the only players sanctioned in 2018, a subsequent cultural review of Australian cricket found a "win at all costs" mentality had pervaded the men's team at the time.
 Current Test captain Pat Cummins, a bowler in the team on the 2018 South Africa tour, admitted the team had an "ugly underbelly" which he vowed to eradicate during his tenure. His predecessor Tim Paine and former coach Justin Langer had also been tasked with changing the team culture.
 "What happened then and continues to play out now has a lot to do with the culture that existed at that time. A culture that CA played a part in creating," Greenberg said.
 "The recognition of that came through the commissioning of the Ethics Centre report and subsequent adoption of 36 of the 42 recommendations.
 "We are indeed proud of the culture that the team has built over the past eight years. Our players and our leaders and our coaches deserve enormous credit for that, in particular Pat (Cummins) and Andrew (McDonald, the current coach) who lead this team with distinction.
 "But we recognise the pain and hurt that events surrounding Sandpapergate have caused."
 In his new memoir, Khawaja alleges sandpaper was used on the ball in the 2018 series' second Test in Port Elizabeth (now Gqeberha) and told Nine newspapers that "it was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us" who were responsible for the plot in Cape Town in the third Test.
 It's a version of events backed by David Warner, who was suspended for 12 months and slapped with a (since revoked) lifetime leadership ban. Back-up bowler Chadd Sayers has also indicated sandpaper was used in Port Elizabeth.  
 Cummins, Nathan Lyon, Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood issued a statement in 2021 denying an implication from Bancroft in an interview with The Guardian that those four frontline bowlers from the Port Elizabeth and Cape Town Tests knew of the plot.
 Cummins recently doubled down on that assertion at press conference in which he fielded questions on the topic for more than an hour.
 "When (Khawaja) says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100 per cent wrong," Cummins said. "I've said that consistently for the last eight years, I did not know that was happening.

 Speaking on Kayo Sports immediately after CA's announcement, Khawaja and Warner were lukewarm in their reactions.
 "I applaud CA for doing this. I wish they did a little bit earlier," said Khawaja. "But there's still some questions to be had, which I'm sure I'll talk to Todd about in the next week.
 "We all want to move on ... The question is, will this allow us to move on? That's the question that has to be asked."
 Neither wanted to see further sanctions handed down, though Warner in particular expressed his desire for "accountability" and "transparency".
 Greenberg insisted the 2018 "investigation has been completed" and that it would not be released publicly given participation in it had been on the condition of confidentiality, adding that eight of the playing XI were interviewed at the time. 
 He added: "The forum is designed where people who weren't interviewed or weren't offered the opportunity in or didn't feel like they had the opportunity to contribute (to the initial investigation) to now contribute. We want to be able to give them the opportunity that they deserve." 
 Greenberg acknowledged the 2018 investigation into the use of sandpaper in Cape Town (and not in previous Tests) had been done quickly given the short turnaround to the fourth Test in Johannesburg. 
 "I've spent a lot of time reading through the reports and the investigation - eight of the 11 players who played that (third) Test match were interviewed. A number of staff were interviewed," he said.
 "People can be critical of what happened there. We won't do that (reopen an investigation) because I think that's unfair and unjust, and it's hard to look through the prism of hindsight.
 "What I do know is that the events conflict with each other, and people's view of the events conflict with each other, and that is probably the most complex part of this. 
 "Anyone who comes in to this forum to provide their views, I would encourage them to be as specific as possible. It's hard to deal with generalities. I am hopeful creating a safe space for players to share their version of events."
